section.title: Unfaithful Israel Called to Repent
section.sectionRationale: This unit turns from indictment to invitation. Having named Judah as more faithless than her already-judged sister Israel, the LORD Himself calls out, return, and pictures a genuine national confession, before closing with the demand that any return be more than words: an inward circumcision of the heart.
section.thesis: Though Judah has proven even more faithless than exiled Israel, the LORD calls both to return, pictures the honest confession true repentance requires, and insists that only a circumcised heart, not mere ritual or words, will avert the coming wrath.
section.frameNote: Four movements: faithless Israel and treacherous Judah compared; the LORD's own call to return; a voice of confession on the barren heights; and the demand to circumcise the heart before disaster falls.

units.label: Faithless Israel, treacherous Judah
units.note: the sister who watched and did not learn

verses.text: Now in the days of King Josiah, the LORD said to me, “Have you seen what faithless Israel has done? She has gone up on every high hill and under every green tree to prostitute herself there.
I thought that after she had done all these things, she would return to Me. But she did not return, and her unfaithful sister Judah saw it.
She saw that because faithless Israel had committed adultery, I gave her a certificate of divorce and sent her away. Yet that unfaithful sister Judah had no fear and prostituted herself as well.
Indifferent to her own infidelity, Israel had defiled the land and committed adultery with stones and trees.
Yet in spite of all this, her unfaithful sister Judah did not return to Me with all her heart, but only in pretense,” declares the LORD.
And the LORD said to me, “Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than unfaithful Judah.

units.label: The LORD's own call to return
units.note: shepherds after His heart, if only they will come

verses.text:
Go, proclaim this message toward the north: 
‘{{shuv|Return}}, O faithless Israel,’ declares the LORD. ‘I will no longer look on you with anger, for I am merciful,’ declares the LORD. ‘I will not be angry forever.

Only acknowledge your guilt, that you have rebelled against the LORD your God. You have scattered your favors to foreign gods under every green tree 
and have not obeyed My voice,’” declares the LORD.
“Return, O faithless children,” declares the LORD, “for I am your master, and I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and bring you to Zion.
Then I will give you shepherds after My own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.”

“In those days, when you multiply and increase in the land,” declares the LORD, “they will no longer discuss the ark of the covenant of the LORD. It will never come to mind, and no one will remember it or miss it, nor will another one be made.

At that time Jerusalem will be called The Throne of the LORD, and all the nations will be gathered in Jerusalem to honor the name of the LORD. They will no longer follow the stubbornness of their evil hearts.
In those days the house of Judah will walk with the house of Israel, and they will come together from the land of the north to the land that I gave to your fathers as an inheritance.

units.label: A voice on the barren heights

verses.text: Then I said, ‘How I long to make you My sons and give you a desirable land, the most beautiful inheritance of all the nations!’ I thought you would call Me ‘Father’ and never turn away from following Me.
But as a woman may betray her husband, so you have betrayed Me, O house of Israel,” declares the LORD.
A voice is heard on the barren heights, the children of Israel weeping and begging for mercy, because they have perverted their ways and forgotten the LORD their God.

“Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness.” 
“Here we are. We come to You, for You are the LORD our God.
Surely deception comes from the hills, and commotion from the mountains. Surely the salvation of Israel is in the LORD our God.
From our youth, that shameful god has consumed what our fathers have worked for, their flocks and herds, their sons and daughters.

Let us lie down in our shame; let our disgrace cover us. We have sinned against the LORD our God, both we and our fathers; from our youth even to this day we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God.”

units.label: Circumcise your hearts
units.note: true repentance is inward before it is outward

verses.text: “If you will return, O Israel, return to Me,” declares the LORD. “If you will remove your detestable idols from My sight and no longer waver,
and if you can swear, ‘As surely as the LORD lives,’ in truth, in justice, and in righteousness, then the nations will be blessed by Him, and in Him they will glory.”

For this is what the LORD says to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: 
“Break up your unplowed ground, and do not sow among the thorns.

{{mul_lev|Circumcise yourselves}} to the LORD, and remove the foreskins of your hearts, 
O men of Judah and people of Jerusalem. Otherwise, My wrath will break out like fire and burn with no one to extinguish it, 
because of your evil deeds.”

shuv.gloss: To turn, return, repent. Repeated insistently across this passage, it is Jeremiah's central word for the change God actually requires: not a ritual gesture but a full turning back of life, worship, and loyalty toward the LORD.

mul_lev.gloss: To circumcise the heart. Physical circumcision marked outward covenant membership; here God demands the inward reality it was always meant to signify, a heart cut free from stubborn self-rule, language later picked up by Moses, Paul, and the promise of a new covenant.

basic.context: God compares Judah unfavorably to her already-exiled sister, the northern kingdom Israel: Israel sinned and was sent away, yet Judah watched that judgment and sinned even more brazenly, offering only a pretend repentance. And yet, astonishingly, the LORD Himself keeps calling, return, promising mercy and even picturing a scene where the people finally confess honestly, before insisting that real change must be internal.
basic.hermeneutics: This is prophetic covenant language using a real historical comparison, the earlier fall of the northern kingdom, to make a moral point about Judah's greater guilt. The honest hard question is why God pictures a confession in 3:21-25 that the rest of the book shows Judah never actually makes; the answer is that this is an invitation and a template for genuine repentance, not a report that it happened, and Judah's continuing unfaithfulness afterward proves the invitation was real but refused.
basic.originalLanguages: Shuv, return, tolls through this passage like a summons, God's own repeated plea rather than a demand issued once and withdrawn. The passage closes with the demand to circumcise, mul, the heart, taking the covenant sign that marked Israel outwardly and insisting it must cut something inward, stubborn self-rule, or it means nothing.
basic.typology: The call to circumcise the heart anticipates Moses' own promise in Deuteronomy 30:6 that God Himself will one day circumcise His people's hearts, a promise fulfilled in the new covenant and the gift of the Spirit, Romans 2:29. The gathering of scattered Israel and Judah under shepherds after God's own heart anticipates the one Shepherd, Christ, who unites His scattered flock.
basic.christ: Paul explicitly redefines true circumcision as a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not the letter, Romans 2:29, fulfilling exactly what Jeremiah 4:4 demands but the Old Covenant could not produce apart from the Spirit poured out through Christ. Jesus is the shepherd after God's own heart promised in 3:15, gathering one flock from Israel and the nations, John 10:16.
basic.god: God is patient beyond what Judah's repeated failures deserve, calling return again and again even after naming her guilt plainly and comparing her unfavorably to a sister already judged. Yet His patience is not indifference: the passage ends with a real warning that unextinguished wrath will fall if the heart itself is not changed.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that the LORD Himself will circumcise Israel's heart to love Him fully. Romans 2:28-29 defines true circumcision as inward, of the heart, by the Spirit. Ezekiel 36:26-27 promises a new heart and God's own Spirit within His people. John 10:16 has Jesus gather one flock under one shepherd, echoing 3:15 and 3:18.
basic.oneStory: This is God's patient, repeated call to a people who keep answering with pretense rather than real change, insisting that true repentance must reach the heart itself. That demand, met only partly under the old covenant, is finally fulfilled when God gives His people new hearts and His own Spirit through Christ, the good shepherd who gathers His scattered flock.

context.literary:
The unit is a single movement with four panels, and it can be read as a conversation in which the LORD does most of the talking and the people are given a few lines to say. The first panel, 3:6 to 11, is a report: two sisters, one judged and one watching. The second, 3:12 to 18, is a sudden turn into speech, a call toward the north and a promise that runs further than the call requires. The third, 3:19 to 25, begins with the LORD's own longing and then lets the people speak, first in a weeping voice on the hills and then in the confession God supplies. The last, 4:1 to 4, takes the people's words and sets conditions on them: if you return, return to Me.

The repetition is the structure. Forms of the verb shuv, turn or return, run through the whole unit, at 3:7, 10, 12, 14, 19, 22 and 4:1, and a related noun is applied to the people as a name. At the centre of the unit stands the single imperative, 'Return', at 3:12, 3:14 and 3:22. The unit is therefore built like a summons that is issued three times and then answered, almost as in a liturgy.

Another thread is the family vocabulary. Sisters in 3:7 to 10, children in 3:14 and 3:19 and 3:22, a husband in 3:14 and 3:20, a father in 3:19. The marriage picture of the previous oracle gives way to a household in which the offended husband is also a parent. In 3:19 the LORD sounds like a father whose hopes for his sons have been disappointed.

The unit ends with two agricultural commands in 4:3, break up unplowed ground, do not sow among thorns, then the sharpest line, 4:4. The poem moves from a courtroom, to a family, to a field, to a body, and in each setting it keeps pressing for the same thing: not a gesture, but a change of the self.
context.historical:
The oracle is introduced as belonging to 'the days of King Josiah', 3:6, and that date matters. Josiah's reform was under way, and it reached beyond Judah: he pulled down the altar at Bethel, which Jeroboam had set up, and cleared the shrines in the cities of Samaria, 2 Kings 23:15 and 19. Jeremiah's call to the north in 3:12 is therefore not poetic fantasy. There were still Israelites in the old northern land, and a pious king was reaching toward them.

The northern kingdom had fallen to Assyria in about 722 BC. Its people were carried off to Halah, Gozan and the cities of the Medes, 2 Kings 17:6, and the 'certificate of divorce' of 3:8 is the prophet's name for that deportation. The vocabulary comes from Deuteronomy 24:1 and from Isaiah 50:1, which also speaks of a certificate of divorce, and means that Israel's exile is the formal result of her unfaithfulness, not a mere defeat in war. Judah saw it happen. For over a century she had watched the northern neighbour destroyed and had learned nothing, which is Jeremiah's point.

The ark, which 3:16 says will be forgotten, was the central object of temple worship, believed to be the footstool of the LORD's throne. Josiah had restored the temple and its worship, and the people valued it deeply, as the temple sermon of Jeremiah 7:4 makes clear when it records the slogan 'the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.' Telling a nation that the ark would one day not be missed was a staggering statement, and it is made in the context of promise: the whole city will be the throne.

The remark about circumcision in 4:4 would have been heard against a world in which Israel's neighbours also circumcised. Jeremiah 9:25 and 26 lists Egypt, Edom, Ammon and Moab as circumcised nations in the flesh and then says all of them, and Israel, are uncircumcised in heart. The sign meant nothing by itself, and Jeremiah's hearers knew it was the thing that marked them off from the Philistines. To tell them that it had no force without the heart was an attack on their confidence.
context.canonical:
This is the passage in the Old Testament where the call to repent is most clearly set beside a promise of what God will do. The command to circumcise the heart comes from Deuteronomy 10:16, 'Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more,' and Deuteronomy 30:6 reverses the verb: 'The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts.' The command and the promise are two ends of the same covenant, and Jeremiah 4:4 stands at the first end. The tension is resolved in Jeremiah 31:31 to 34 and Ezekiel 36:26 and 27, where God Himself writes the law on the heart and gives a new heart and spirit.

The reunion of Israel and Judah in 3:18 prepares for Ezekiel's two sticks joined as one in Ezekiel 37:15 to 22 and for Jeremiah's own promise of a new covenant with 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah', Jeremiah 31:31. The shepherds 'after My own heart' of 3:15 echo David, in whom the LORD found a man after His own heart, 1 Samuel 13:14, and lead to the promise of a righteous Branch in Jeremiah 23:1 to 6 and the shepherd David of Ezekiel 34:23.

The New Testament makes use of nearly every line. Paul says that a Jew is one inwardly and that circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, Romans 2:28 and 29, and that what counts is a new creation, Galatians 6:15. Stephen accuses the council of having uncircumcised hearts and ears, Acts 7:51, in a line straight out of Jeremiah and Leviticus 26:41. Paul says believers were circumcised in Christ, Colossians 2:11, and Peter, at the Jerusalem council, says that God cleansed Gentile hearts by faith, Acts 15:8 and 9. In John 10:16 Jesus speaks of other sheep that are not of this fold and one flock, and Revelation 21:22 to 24 describes a city in which God and the Lamb are the temple and the nations walk by its light, the fulfilment of the 'Throne of the LORD' of 3:17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The editor who placed this unit beside the previous one wanted two things heard together. The first is that Judah's response to the fall of the north had been a kind of acting, 'only in pretense', 3:10. The second is that this did not exhaust the LORD's patience. The reader is meant to feel the pity before the anger. The comparison with the northern sister, whom the text calls 'more righteous', is aimed at a people who thought their survival proved their virtue.

The oracle is also written for people already in exile, who would read it afterward. To them it says that return was possible because the LORD had always called for it, and that the call to the north in 3:12 had not been withdrawn when the north was lost. Exiles in Babylon who heard 3:14, 'one from a city and two from a family', could take comfort that numbers were not an obstacle. The text invites the reader to see the confession of 3:22 to 25 as words they might make their own.

Finally, 4:1 to 4 insists on what real return looks like. It must be to Him, 4:1, in truth, justice and righteousness, 4:2, from the heart, 4:4. The author did not want the invitation heard as cheap grace. The people were meant to take it seriously enough to see that God's mercy and God's demand run together.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records God's words to a particular people in a particular decade and it describes a comparison between two kingdoms that no longer exist. It does not teach that the exile of the north was worse or better than any later calamity, and it does not set a rule for ranking nations by their religious record. The statement that Israel was 'more righteous' than Judah is a rhetorical statement about relative guilt, not a verdict on the north's overall character, which the prophets elsewhere describe as grievous.

What is prescribed is a pattern of repentance. Return must be to the LORD Himself, it must be total, and it must reach the inner life. The confession of 3:22 to 25 gives a template: 'We come to You', an acknowledgment that the idol's promise was deception, the admission that guilt runs back through the fathers, and the willingness to lie down in shame. It is meant to be learned and used, though the book warns that saying such words is not the same as meaning them. The promise that God will heal faithlessness is also an encouragement for the present, but it should not be turned into a guarantee that earthly consequences will be removed once a person repents.

debates.question: Does 4:2 say the nations will 'be blessed' or 'bless themselves'?

views.label: The nations will be blessed through Israel
views.case: The BSB reads, 'then the nations will be blessed by Him, and in Him they will glory.' This takes the promise of Genesis 12:3, that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham's line, as being picked up here. A repentant Israel would be the channel for blessing the nations.

views.label: The nations will bless themselves by Him
views.case: The Hebrew verb is in the reflexive stem, the one used in Genesis 22:18 and 26:4, and some versions render it 'bless themselves'. On this reading the nations will use the LORD's name as the standard of blessing, saying in effect, 'May we be blessed as Israel is.' It still assumes the nations come to the LORD, but it gives them more of the initiative.

views.label: A deliberate blend
views.case: Others think the ambiguity is the point: the stem the writer chose is the one that already carries both senses in the patriarchal texts, so that the prophet echoes the whole Abrahamic promise instead of one reading of it.

debates.bearing: On any of these readings the verse links Israel's repentance to the blessing of the nations, which is what the Abrahamic promise intended, and it fits with 3:17, where all nations gather in Jerusalem to honour the LORD.

debates.question: What does it mean that the ark 'will never come to mind'?

views.label: God's presence will be wider than one object
views.case: Verse 17 immediately says that Jerusalem will be called the Throne of the LORD. The ark was the footstool of the throne, and the promise is that the whole city will take its place. The ark is not despised, but it is not missed.

views.label: A warning against trust in sacred objects
views.case: Jeremiah 7:4 mocks those who chant 'the temple of the LORD' as though the building were a charm. Read with that, 3:16 is a promise that the day will come when Israel will not need a symbol to ensure the LORD's presence, because the heart will be changed.

views.label: A glimpse of the new covenant age
views.case: Many Christians read it as looking forward to a time when God's presence is not tied to a place, as in Revelation 21:22, where there is no temple because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple.

debates.bearing: The three readings share the point that the ark's absence is a sign of fullness, not loss. The text speaks of it without any grief.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb shuv does most of the work in this passage, and the passage plays with its two directions, turning back toward God and turning away from Him. The Hebrew of 3:6, 8, 11 and 12 calls Israel meshuvah, and Judah is called bogedah, treacherous. The BSB renders the first as 'faithless', which loses the sound. Meshuvah is formed from shuv, so the northern kingdom is, in effect, called 'the Turning-Away'. The pun reaches a climax in 3:22: 'Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness.' The command is shuvu, the children are shovavim, and the healing is of their meshuvot. God says in effect, 'Turn back, you turners-away, and I will cure your turning-away.' The very word that names their problem is used to name their cure.

In 3:14 the LORD says 'I am your master'. The verb is baal, the word that means to own, to be master of, or to be married to, and it is also the name of the rival god. The same form is used in 31:32, where the BSB has 'though I was a husband to them'. In both verses the LORD claims, in the vocabulary of the rival, the real relationship of a husband, and so takes the word back from Baal.

The people's reply in 3:24 calls Baal 'that shameful god'. The Hebrew word is bosheth, shame, and Israel's tradition used it as a replacement for the name Baal in some personal names. Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel 2:8 is called Esh-baal in 1 Chronicles 8:33, and Jeremiah 11:13, which the BSB renders 'the altars of shame', takes the same step. The confession lets the people say what the idol really was, a shame that consumed their flocks and sons.

In 3:10 the BSB reads 'only in pretense'. The Hebrew is sheqer, falsehood or deception, and the same word recurs in 3:23, 'Surely deception comes from the hills', the shrines on the high places. Real repentance is the opposite of both. In 3:9 the BSB has 'indifferent', where older translations such as the King James Version read 'through the lightness of her whoredom'; the Hebrew is difficult, and the point either way is that Israel treated adultery as a trifle.

The word in 4:1 for 'waver' belongs to the family of nud, to wander or shake, and is related to the wandering that was Cain's sentence in Genesis 4:12. Those who drift from the LORD become wanderers. And in 4:3 the 'unplowed ground' is the Hebrew nir, a fallow field, the same term that Hosea 10:12 uses in a plea to break up the fallow ground. The three adverbs that qualify the oath in 4:2, truth, justice and righteousness, are the qualities that Jeremiah 5:1 and 9:24 go looking for.

The last image of 4:4 is the circumcision of the foreskin of the heart. The Hebrew has two words, mul, to circumcise, and orlah, the foreskin. Genesis 17:11 uses the same pair for the sign of the covenant in the flesh. Jeremiah applies them to what the flesh was meant to signify.

typology.fulfillment: Israel's physical sign pointed to a cut that only God could make. Moses spoke of the LORD circumcising the heart, Deuteronomy 30:6, and Paul says the true circumcision is of the heart by the Spirit, Romans 2:29. In Christ believers are 'circumcised in the putting off of your sinful nature', Colossians 2:11, and Philippians 3:3 says that we are the circumcision who worship by the Spirit and put no confidence in the flesh. The type falls short in that the outward sign could be performed by human hands, whereas Christ's circumcision is not.

The failed shepherds of 2:8 are replaced by shepherds who feed the people with knowledge and understanding. The final answer is Christ, who says 'I am the good shepherd' and lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and who is called the Chief Shepherd, 1 Peter 5:4. Ezekiel 34:11 to 16 promises that the LORD Himself will seek His scattered flock, which is what Jesus claims to do in Luke 19:10. The type falls short because the shepherds of Jeremiah's promise could fail; the Shepherd who dies for the flock does not.

typology.type: The reunion of Israel and Judah, Jeremiah 3:18
typology.fulfillment: The divided sisters come back together from the north to the land of inheritance. Ezekiel pictures two sticks made one, Ezekiel 37:15 to 22, and Jesus says that He has other sheep not of this fold and there will be one flock and one shepherd, John 10:16. Paul says that Christ has broken down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile and made the two one, Ephesians 2:14 to 16. The type is incomplete because the reunion in Jeremiah is of two parts of one nation, but the reunion in Christ includes the nations.

typology.type: Jerusalem as the Throne of the LORD, Jeremiah 3:17
typology.fulfillment: The place of the ark becomes a city, and the city gathers the nations. This points forward to a presence that no longer needs a building, Revelation 21:22 to 24, and to Jesus' statement that true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, John 4:23. The type is imperfect since earthly Jerusalem was still a place with walls, but the Jerusalem to come is described as a bride and a city whose temple is God Himself.

study.christ:
Chapter 3 contains no direct prophecy of a person, but its logic needs one. The call of the LORD is 'Return', and the answer given by the people is a confession that they cannot make unaided. The text itself shows this: the confession in 3:22 to 25 is put in their mouths by God, and the demand of 4:4 asks for something that, according to Deuteronomy 29:4, the LORD had not yet given, 'a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear.' The gap between what is demanded and what people can do is what the New Testament says Christ closes.

The heart is the first meeting place. Jeremiah himself later asks who can understand the human heart, which is 'deceitful above all things and beyond cure', 17:9, and then promises that God will write His law on it, 31:33. The New Testament says that this is done by Christ and the Spirit. Paul writes that the circumcision of the heart is by the Spirit and not by the written code, Romans 2:29. At the Jerusalem council Peter says that God cleansed Gentile hearts by faith, Acts 15:9. In Colossians 2:11 the circumcision made without hands is the circumcision of Christ, which Paul links to burial and resurrection in the next verse. The cut that Jeremiah asked for is finally made in the person of the one who was cut off for His people, Isaiah 53:8.

The shepherd theme leads the same way. The promise of 3:15 is not simply for a better class of leader. It speaks of shepherds who feed the flock with knowledge and understanding, and it is picked up in the promise of a righteous Branch, Jeremiah 23:5 and 6. Jesus claims to be the good shepherd who lays down His life, John 10:11, and who has other sheep to bring, John 10:16, and the picture of a scattered flock gathered from north and south is exactly that of 3:18.

The love behind the offer also needs a source. The LORD says in 3:19, 'How I long to make you My sons', and this longing is shown without reserve when the Son comes. The parable in Luke 15:20, in which the father sees his son 'while he was still in the distance' and runs, is the living out of the verse, 'I will not be angry forever.' Jesus tells that parable as a window into the Father's heart, and then goes to a cross so that the Father's welcome would not be at the expense of justice.

Caution is needed. The passage does not prove that Jeremiah foresaw the cross, and it should not be read as if every verse hides a prophecy. What it shows is a need that grows sharper the more it is pressed, and the New Testament presents Christ as the answer that fits the need.
study.god:
The LORD of this passage is first of all a God who goes on speaking. The most surprising feature is that He keeps calling. After the diagnosis of 3:6 to 11, He might have fallen silent, and instead He says 'Go, proclaim this message toward the north,' 3:12, and sends the prophet after the people who have been exiled for a century. A divine mercy that reaches across the years is not an afterthought. The adjective in 3:12, 'I am merciful', is from the same family as the covenant love of the Old Testament, and its sense is loyal, faithful love. He is merciful because He has bound Himself to them.

His anger is real and also bounded. 'I will not be angry forever,' He says, which recalls the self-description of Exodus 34:6, 'slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.' Yet 4:4 closes with the same fire as an alternative: 'My wrath will break out like fire and burn with no one to extinguish it.' The passage does not choose between mercy and wrath. It makes them two responses to the same people, and says the human response decides which one they meet. It also does not say that God's wrath is a mood that passes by itself. Its removal requires acknowledgment and return.

The passage shows a God who wants the person and not only the behaviour. 'Only acknowledge your guilt', 3:13, asks for honesty. 'Return to Me', 4:1, asks for relationship. 'Circumcise yourselves', 4:4, asks for a changed heart. This is a God who sees, as 17:10 says, the heart and the mind, and who is therefore not deceived by the reforms of Josiah's time or the pretence of Judah. He knows when worship is only in pretense, and He knows the difference.

He is also a God who plans beyond the present. In 3:15 to 18 He looks forward to a time when shepherds are faithful, when the ark is not missed, when nations gather, and when the divided people are one. The same Lord who shames Judah speaks of what He will do for her, and the future is stated as His own work: 'I will take you', 'I will give you shepherds.' The hope does not rest on Israel's performance.

For worship, the passage gives a model of how to come back. The confession in 3:22 to 25 begins with 'Here we are. We come to You, for You are the LORD our God.' It says that the high places were a deception, that salvation is in Him alone, that shame is deserved, and that guilt is inherited and shared. It is a prayer for any believer who needs to return, and the God who composes it for them wants it said.

crossReferences.note: The law that a husband may not take back a wife who has been married to another is the rule behind Jeremiah 3:1, and the divorce certificate of 3:8 comes from the same chapter. Jeremiah applies it to Israel and Judah, and then has God offer a return the law would normally forbid.

Isaiah uses the same legal image of a certificate of divorce, and asks where it is. The answer in Isaiah is that the mother was sent away for her own sins, as Jeremiah says of Israel, but in both prophets the divorce is not the last word.

The fall of Samaria, with the deportation to Halah, Gozan and the cities of the Medes, is the event the 'certificate of divorce' names. It supplies the history behind 3:8 and shows why the call 'toward the north' in 3:12 is aimed at real exiles.

Ezekiel names the sisters Oholah for Samaria and Oholibah for Jerusalem, and tells the same story at greater length. It confirms that Jeremiah's pair of sisters is a standing prophetic image of the two kingdoms.

The people are commanded to circumcise their hearts and stiffen their necks no more. Jeremiah's 4:4 is the same demand in the same words, and shows that the call to inner change was already present in the Law.

The LORD Himself will circumcise the hearts of the people and their descendants so that they love Him. This is the promise that completes the command of 4:4, and it points to the new covenant of Jeremiah 31.

Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon and Moab are all circumcised in the flesh yet 'uncircumcised', and the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart. This shows that the sign carried no advantage by itself and that Jeremiah meant 4:4 as a leveling of Israel with the nations.

Hosea's closing call, 'Return, O Israel', gives words to say and promises, 'I will heal their apostasy', and 'I will freely love them'. It is the nearest parallel to the confession and healing of Jeremiah 3:22.

'Break up your unplowed ground' is the same phrase that Jeremiah uses in 4:3, with the promise that the LORD will rain righteousness on the broken soil. The parallel shows that preparing the field is a recognised image for repentance in the prophets.

The promise that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham underlies 4:2, where the nations are to be blessed by the LORD or bless themselves by Him. The verse ties a repentant Israel to the purpose for which she was chosen.
Two sticks, one for Judah and one for Ephraim, are joined in the prophet's hand as a sign that the two kingdoms will be one nation under one king. This is the fuller picture of the reunion of 3:18.

Paul says that circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, and that praise comes from God and not from men. He draws directly on Jeremiah 4:4 and Deuteronomy 30:6, and applies the principle to both Jews and Gentiles.

study.oneStory:
The shape of this passage is the shape of the whole Bible's account of what is wrong with us and what God does about it. In Genesis 3 humanity was unfaithful in a garden. In Genesis 12 God began to bless the nations through one family. In Exodus 19 He made that family a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The story told here, of two sisters who left their husband, is the story of how the family chosen to bless the nations kept failing at the thing it was chosen for. The nations were meant to be drawn to the LORD by the sight of a faithful people, and Jeremiah 4:2 still holds that outcome out.

The passage also answers the question the early chapters of Genesis left open: can anyone return? Cain went east and became a wanderer, Genesis 4:12 and 16. Humanity at Babel scattered, Genesis 11:8. Israel is scattered too, and the LORD calls toward the north, which is the direction of the exile. The pattern is the same, a people dispersed because of unfaithfulness, and the call is the same: come back. What is new is that the scatterer is also the gatherer, 3:14, 'I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and bring you to Zion.'

It looks ahead with unusual clarity. The law of the heart that the Torah commanded and could not produce becomes, in Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36, a gift, and the ministry of the Spirit under the new covenant is how it arrives. The shepherds after God's heart are given in the one Shepherd. The reunion of the sisters becomes, in Christ, the joining of Jew and Gentile into one people, Ephesians 2:14 to 16. The ark's absence points to the temple that is the Lord God and the Lamb, Revelation 21:22.

And it ends where Scripture ends. The city that is called the Throne of the LORD in 3:17 is the city that comes down out of heaven in Revelation 21, where the nations walk by its light and bring in their glory, Revelation 21:24. The bride who left her husband and was spoken of as divorced is prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband, Revelation 21:2. The call to return, issued over and over to a people who would not, is finally answered by a people the LORD Himself has made able to return, and the long story of turning away ends with all things turned toward Him.

quiz.q: How does God compare Judah to her sister Israel in this passage?

options.text: Judah has proven even more faithless, sinning further despite watching Israel's judgment.
options.note: Verse 11 explicitly states that faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah.

options.text: Judah was innocent while Israel alone was guilty.
options.note: The passage explicitly indicts Judah as worse, not innocent.

options.text: Both were equally faithful to the covenant.
options.note: Neither kingdom is described as faithful; Judah is described as the more unfaithful of the two.

options.text: Judah repented while Israel refused to.
options.note: The passage says the opposite: Judah only pretended to return, verse 10, while Israel's judgment had already fallen.

quiz.q: What does God repeatedly call His people to do in Jeremiah 3:12-22?

options.text: Return, promising mercy and healing rather than endless anger.
options.note: The Hebrew shuv, return, is repeated as the LORD's own invitation, paired with the promise, I will heal your faithlessness.

options.text: Rebuild the temple immediately.
options.note: The call is to return in heart and loyalty, not a building project.

options.text: Seek alliances with Egypt and Assyria.
options.note: Such alliances are condemned elsewhere in Jeremiah, not commanded here.

options.text: Wait silently for judgment without any response.
options.note: The passage actively calls for a response, return, not passive silence.

quiz.q: What does the confession in Jeremiah 3:21-25 model?

options.text: Honest acknowledgment of guilt and shame rather than excuses.
options.note: The voice says, let us lie down in our shame, we have sinned, a template of unflinching honesty before God.

options.text: A demand that God explain Himself before they will repent.
options.note: The confession contains no demand of God; it is pure acknowledgment of guilt.

options.text: Blaming their ancestors entirely and excusing themselves.
options.note: The confession includes both we and our fathers, not shifting blame away from the speakers themselves.

options.text: A promise to build more altars to foreign gods.
options.note: This is the opposite of the passage's point; the confession renounces, not embraces, idolatry.

quiz.q: What does God demand in Jeremiah 4:4, and why does it matter?

options.text: Circumcising the heart, showing that real repentance must be inward, not merely outward.
options.note: This demand insists true change must reach beneath ritual and words to the heart itself.

options.text: Literal circumcision performed publicly as a display.
options.note: Circumcision was already an established covenant sign; the demand here is explicitly that it be applied to the heart, not merely the body.

options.text: Building new altars in every town.
options.note: The passage calls for removing idols, not building new worship sites.

options.text: Paying a temple tax to avert judgment.
options.note: The passage is about inward repentance, not a financial transaction.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament fulfill the demand to circumcise the heart?

options.text: Paul teaches that true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, fulfilled through Christ.
options.note: Romans 2:28-29 directly answers Jeremiah's demand, showing it fulfilled through the Spirit given in Christ.

options.text: It has no connection to anything in the New Testament.
options.note: Paul explicitly develops this very theme in Romans 2.

options.text: It refers only to circumcision requirements for gentile converts.
options.note: Paul's point is broader: true circumcision is inward and spiritual for all believers, not merely a debate over gentile practice.

options.text: It is fulfilled only in a future, still-unrealized age.
options.note: Paul presents the circumcised heart as a present reality through the Spirit, not merely a future hope.

questions: God says Judah watched Israel's judgment and sinned anyway, even more brazenly. What warnings from others' consequences have you seen and ignored in your own life?
God calls return again and again, promising mercy rather than endless anger. Where do you assume God's patience with you has run out, when His own words here say otherwise?
The pictured confession is honest: we have sinned, both we and our fathers. Where are you tempted to explain away sin rather than simply naming it?
God demands a circumcised heart, not merely outward compliance. Where in your life have you settled for looking repentant rather than actually being changed?

This passage insists that real repentance reaches the heart before it reaches behavior. What would it look like this week to let God change your heart first, rather than trying to fix your behavior on your own?

translationNotes.note: The certificate of divorce alludes to Deuteronomy 24:1-3, formal legal language for ending a marriage, applied metaphorically to the LORD's judgment on the northern kingdom's exile.

The statement that the ark of the covenant will no longer be missed or remade points to a future so transformed by God's presence that the old symbol of that presence becomes unnecessary, not a devaluing of the ark in its own time.

Circumcise yourselves to the LORD uses the covenant sign of Genesis 17 metaphorically; the demand is for the heart itself to be cut free from stubbornness, language Moses had already used in Deuteronomy 10:16.
